original_text:
Interviewer:
"You have a Spark job writing 200GB of Parquet data daily to S3. After 3 months, queries become painfully slow. Nothing in the code changed. What happened?"

Candidate:
"This sounds like the Small Files Problem."

Interviewer:
"Explain."

Candidate:
"If the job writes too many small Parquet files, over time we end up with millions of tiny files in S3.

Each file adds:
Metadata overhead
Task scheduling overhead
File open/close costing
S3 listing latency
Instead of processing data, Spark spends time managing files."

Interviewer:
"How would you fix it?"

Candidate:
"I’d focus on file size optimization:

• Tune spark.sql.shuffle.partitions
• Use repartition() or coalesce() carefully before writes
• Target optimal file sizes (128MB–1GB depending on workload)
• Enable optimized writes (Delta Lake)
• Run periodic compaction jobs

The goal isn’t fewer partitions — it’s properly sized files."

Interviewer:
"What if reducing partitions causes executor OOM?"

Candidate:
"Then we balance compute and storage. Instead of forcing large partitions, we rely on controlled compaction and adaptive execution."

Interviewer:
"What’s the real lesson?"

Candidate:
"In Big Data, performance problems are often storage layout problems — not compute problems."

Interviewer:
"You are hired."

ai_analysis.summary: The post presents an interview scenario in which a Spark job writes 200GB of Parquet data daily to S3, and queries become painfully slow after three months without a code change. It identifies the Small Files Problem: too many small Parquet files can produce millions of tiny files in S3, adding metadata, task scheduling, file open/close, and S3 listing overhead. Recommended remedies include tuning spark.sql.shuffle.partitions, using repartition() or coalesce() carefully before writes, targeting file sizes of 128MB–1GB depending on the workload, enabling optimized writes with Delta Lake, and running periodic compaction jobs. If reducing partitions causes executor OOM, the post recommends balancing compute and storage through controlled compaction and adaptive execution rather than forcing large partitions. Its central lesson is that Big Data performance problems are often storage-layout problems rather than compute problems.
